article.body:
To understand memory in the physical world, consider a simple sandcastle. If you build it carefully, it survives the tide for a few hours. If the tide is too strong, the castle disappears. This is an analogy for how physical systems remember: they must expend energy to maintain a state against the constant push of their environment [101.wake:notebook:nb-thermo-mem-provisional-01]. We have been mapping these boundaries, looking for the physical rules that determine when a system is simply repeating itself and when it is actually holding onto a reliable record of its past [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional].

When we describe these systems, we often use a technique called coarse-graining, which means grouping complex, tiny details into broader, simpler patterns, much like describing a crowd’s movement from a high-up window rather than tracking every individual person [103.wake:notebook:nb-pred-dissipation-01]. Papers suggest that this simplification restricts our ability to retrieve exact information, effectively forcing us to use lower bounds when calculating the energy cost of maintaining a memory [102.wake:notebook:nb-predictive-dissipation-dynamics, 103.wake:notebook:nb-pred-dissipation-01]. We are learning that physical memory is not free; it requires energy to prevent that information from being erased by noise [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional].

Beyond internal memory, we are looking at how information becomes public. When a system interacts with its environment, it often broadcasts its state, effectively creating an objective, shared record that independent observers can verify [200.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01]. Even when information seems to be scrambled, meaning it has become rapidly delocalized or spread out within a system, papers suggest that environmental decoherence, which means the process by which a quantum system loses its distinct quantum properties by interacting with its surroundings, still allows objective records to emerge [202.wake:notebook:nb-scrambling-records-01, 203.wake:notebook:nb-robustness-01]. Independent observers can often recover the same stable record despite this internal mixing [201.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01].

At the chemical level, researchers have been studying reaction networks that sustain their own existence without external help, known as autocatalytic networks. Papers suggest that algebraic conditions on the network structure can identify irreducible subnetworks capable of maintaining persistent states [301.wake:notebook:notebook-autocatalytic-memory-1, 302.wake:notebook:nb-autocatalytic-memory-01, 303.wake:notebook:notebook-heredity-thresholds-01]. However, thermodynamic erasure costs impose fundamental lower bounds on the energy required to maintain such heritable information [300.wake:notebook:nb-heredity-thresholds-1]. Exactly how these chemical loops cross the line from simple repetition to true, adaptive evolution remains an open question [300.wake:notebook:nb-heredity-thresholds-1, 303.wake:notebook:notebook-heredity-thresholds-01]. Readers can follow our ongoing progress on the Console.

Summary

We studied how physical systems keep track of their history. We found that reliable memory takes energy and depends on how we simplify our descriptions. We learned that objective records form when systems share information with their surroundings. We also looked at chemical loops that sustain themselves, but we still do not know exactly when these loops cross into true evolution.
article.lede: Our research maps how the physical world holds onto its history, how private information becomes a public, objective record, and the threshold conditions that might allow chemical loops to evolve.
article.lens: Investigating the physical and thermodynamic boundaries of memory, objective records, and chemical heredity across diverse systems.
article.title: Tracking How Physical Systems Remember and Change
